text: The digestive tract runs from the beak to the cloaca. Food is picked up by the beak and enters the mouth; chickens have no teeth and cannot chew, so the tongue pushes feed to the back of the mouth to be swallowed. In ducks, the beak is shaped for scooping up water and searching the ground for insects and other food; the nostrils sit near the head end of the bill so the duck can find food in water without holding its breath. After the mouth, the digestive tube continues: the esophagus is a flexible tube carrying food to the crop and proventriculus; the crop is an out-pocketing of the esophagus used to store feed; the proventriculus is the chicken's 'true' stomach; the gizzard is the 'mechanical stomach', made of strong muscle and can contain small pebbles that grind the grain; the small intestine begins with the duodenum, which receives secretions from the pancreas and liver via the gall bladder; the ceca are two blind pouches located where the small and large intestines join; the large intestine is shorter than the small intestine; and the cloaca is where digestive wastes mix with urinary wastes before leaving the body.
